The problem asks for the minimum number of queries Bob needs to uniquely determine 2021 secret positive integers $x_1, \ldots, x_{2021}$ which are pairwise relatively prime. Bob can choose a subset of indices $S$ and receive the product $P = \prod_{i \in S} x_i$.

Let's analyze the information Bob obtains. Since the integers are pairwise relatively prime, for any prime $p$, $p$ divides at most one of the integers $x_i$. Let $x_i = \prod_{p} p^{v_{i,p}}$. Then for a query set $S$, the product is $P_S = \prod_{i \in S} x_i$. The exponent of a prime $p$ in $P_S$ is $\sum_{i \in S} v_{i,p}$. Since at most one $x_i$ is divisible by $p$, let this index be $k_p$ (if no such $i$ exists, the exponent is 0). Then the exponent of $p$ in $P_S$ is:
$$v_p(P_S) = \begin{cases} v_p(x_{k_p}) & \text{if } k_p \in S \\ 0 & \text{if } k_p \notin S \end{cases}$$
Bob receives the integer $P_S$, and by virtue of factorization (assuming he can determine prime factors), he obtains the sequence of exponents for $P_S$. Specifically, for each prime factor $p$ of $x_{k_p}$, he observes that $p$ divides $P_S$ if and only if $k_p \in S$. Moreover, the multiplicity of $p$ in $P_S$ tells him the exponent $v_p(x_{k_p})$.
Bob needs to determine the integers $x_1, \ldots, x_{2021}$. This means he must identify which prime factors belong to which $x_i$, and their respective exponents.
For a prime $p$ belonging to $x_k$, the "signature" or pattern of which queries contain $k$ determines the source of $p$. Specifically, let $\Sigma_k = \{ t \mid k \in S_t \}$ be the set of query indices that include index $k$. If Bob receives the answers to the queries $S_1, \ldots, S_m$, then for any prime $p$ dividing $x_k$, the observed non-zero valuations (or simply the presence of $p$ in the product) will occur exactly in the queries indexed by $t \in \Sigma_k$. If $x_k$ has no prime factors (i.e., $x_k=1$), it will never appear in any product, so it produces no signals. However, since Bob needs to determine $x_k$ for *any* valid configuration (including cases where $x_k > 1$), he must be able to distinguish $x_k$ from other indices $x_j$.
If two indices $i$ and $j$ have the same signature set $\Sigma_i = \Sigma_j$, then any prime factor of $x_i$ would appear in exactly the same set of queries as any prime factor of $x_j$. Since $x_i$ and $x_j$ are coprime, they can have different prime factors. Bob would be unable to distinguish whether a certain prime factor belonged to $x_i$ or $x_j$ based on the query results. Furthermore, if $\Sigma_i = \emptyset$ (meaning $i$ is never included in any query set), Bob would never see any factor of $x_i$ in the products. Since $x_i$ could be any integer coprime to the others, he could not determine $x_i$ (for instance, $x_i$ could be 1 or any prime not appearing elsewhere, or a composite). Thus, he must query every index at least once.
Therefore, to uniquely identify $x_1, \ldots, x_n$, Bob needs to choose a sequence of $m$ query sets $S_1, \ldots, S_m$ such that the sets of indices included in each query are distinct and non-empty. That is, the columns of the incidence matrix must be distinct and non-zero vectors in $\{0, 1\}^m$.
The number of such distinct non-empty vectors is $2^m - 1$. We require:
$$n \le 2^m - 1 \implies 2^m \ge n + 1$$
Given $n = 2021$, we need to find the smallest integer $m$ satisfying $2^m \ge 2022$.
We calculate powers of 2:
$2^{10} = 1024$
$2^{11} = 2048$
Since $1024 < 2022 \le 2048$, we have $m = 11$.
Bob can construct the queries by assigning each index $k \in \{1, \ldots, 2021\}$ a distinct non-empty signature vector of length 11. He sets $S_t = \{ k \mid \text{the } t\text{-th component of signature } k \text{ is } 1 \}$. With this setup, Bob can distinguish every $x_k$ and determine its prime factorization uniquely from the responses.

Final answer: \boxed{11}<|im_end|>

source.problem: Bob knows that Alice has 2021 secret positive integers $x_{1}, \ldots, x_{2021}$ that are pairwise relatively prime. Bob would like to figure out Alice's integers. He is allowed to choose a set $S \subseteq\{1,2, \ldots, 2021\}$ and ask her for the product of $x_{i}$ over $i \in S$. Alice must answer each of Bob's queries truthfully, and Bob may use Alice's previous answers to decide his next query. Compute the minimum number of queries Bob needs to guarantee that he can figure out each of Alice's integers.
source.solution: In general, Bob can find the values of all $n$ integers asking only $\left\lfloor\log _{2} n\right\rfloor+1$ queries. For each of Alice's numbers $x_{i}$, let $Q_{i}$ be the set of queries $S$ such that $i \in S$. Notice that all $Q_{i}$ must be nonempty and distinct. If there exists an empty $Q_{i}$, Bob has asked no queries that include $x_{i}$ and has no information about its value. If there exist $i, j, i \neq j$ such that $Q_{i}=Q_{j}, x_{i}$ and $x_{j}$ could be interchanged without the answer to any query changing, so there does not exist a unique sequence of numbers described by the answers to Bob's queries (Alice can make her numbers distinct). From the above, $\left\lfloor\log _{2} n\right\rfloor+1$ is a lower bound on the number of queries, because the number of distinct nonempty subsets of $\{1, \ldots, n\}$ is $2^{n}-1$. If Bob asks any set of queries such that all $Q_{i}$ are nonempty and disjoint, he can uniquely determine Alice's numbers. In particular, since the values $x_{1}, \ldots, x_{2021}$ are relatively prime, each prime factor of $x_{i}$ occurs in the answer to query $S_{j}$ iff $j \in Q(i)$ (and that prime factor will occur in each answer exactly to the power with which it appears in the factorization of $x_{i}$ ). Since all $Q(i)$ are unique, all $x_{i}$ can therefore be uniquely recovered by computing the product of the prime powers that occur exactly in the answers to queries $Q(i)$. It is possible for Bob to ask $\left\lfloor\log _{2} n\right\rfloor+1$ queries so that each $i$ is contained in a unique nonempty subset of them. One possible construction is to include the index $i$ in the $j$ th query iff the $2^{i-1}$-value bit is set in the binary representation of $j$. So the answer is $\left\lfloor\log _{2} 2021\right\rfloor+1=11$.
